source: Wallace and Boulton (1968) An information measure for classification, Computer Journal 11(2):185-194
finding: First paper on MML. It introduced the Snob program for unsupervised classification (clustering). The best classification is the one that gives the shortest two-part message: first the classes, then the data given the classes.
numbers: Computer Journal vol 11 no 2 pp 185-194. Paper itself not opened (publisher site blocked); facts come from the Dowe 2008 foreword, the Dowe 2010 chapter and the Snob page.
limits: Founding paper not read first-hand. Treat details of its experiments as unverified here.
agent_relevance: Background: score a hypothesis by (cost of stating it) plus (cost of the data given it). Counts bits, needs no judge.

source: Dowe (2008) Foreword re C. S. Wallace, Computer Journal 51(5):523-560 (quotes Wallace's 2003 talk on Boulton's idea)
finding: The idea came from a meeting of two views. David Boulton, an engineer, saw a theory as a concise way to represent data. Wallace was a Bayesian. They found the two views were the same thing.
numbers: Boulton's example was the periodic table: about 70 elements known at first, 92 later, arranged so that column and row show similarities. Knowing the table saves describing each element.
quote: he had always thought of theories as a way of concisely representing data
limits: Retold from Wallace's talk of 20 Nov 2003; memory-based history written by a close colleague, not a neutral historian.
agent_relevance: Gives the intuition for our agent: a good theory is a short code that makes the data cheap to state.

source: Dowe (2008) Foreword re C. S. Wallace (Wallace's own account of publication delays)
finding: Strict MML was published in 1975, but exposure in the statistics literature was delayed because referees rejected it. One referee found the idea 'repugnant'. A paper in standard statistical language only appeared in 1987, with Peter Freeman's help.
numbers: 1968 first paper; 1975 Strict MML (Wallace and Boulton); 1987 Wallace and Freeman, J Royal Stat Soc B. Wallace's talk: people would resist, then 'everybody'll be doing it'.
limits: Autobiographical; the delay is the claim of the MML camp.
agent_relevance: Shows MML sat outside the statistics mainstream for 20 years; MDL (1978) became better known. Cite MML as the earlier source of the two-part idea.

source: Dowe (2010) MML, hybrid Bayesian network graphical models, statistical consistency, invariance and uniqueness (Handbook of Philosophy of Science vol 7)
finding: Three equivalent ways to see an MML hypothesis: (i) best two-part compression, (ii) most probable hypothesis after seeing data, (iii) the best trade-off between structure and noise. Part 1 states the hypothesis H, part 2 states the data D given H. Length = -log2 Pr(H) - log2 Pr(D|H).
numbers: An event of probability p costs -log2 p bits. Minimising message length equals maximising Pr(H).Pr(D|H). First part captures all the structure, second part holds the noise.
quote: files with structure compress (if our file compression program is able to find said structure)
limits: Written by a leading MML advocate; the framing of MML as the only valid view is partisan.
agent_relevance: This is the exact scoring rule behind a 'shortest explanation wins' check: the program can count bits for hypothesis and for residual.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, section 6.1 Strict MML (SMML)
finding: Strict MML builds a code-book over the data space: it partitions data into groups, each with one estimate, so that the expected two-part length is smallest. The objective is the sum over groups of -q_j log q_j (cost of naming the estimate) plus the q_j-weighted cost of the data given the estimate. It is intractable except in simple cases such as the binomial.
numbers: Formula (18) in the chapter. q_j is the prior probability mass of group j; r(x_i) = integral of h(theta) f(x_i|theta) is a probability, not a density. Intractable because assignment is discrete ('gritty', Wallace).
limits: No general fast algorithm; practical work uses approximations.
agent_relevance: Strict MML is the ideal; an agent can only use approximations such as Wallace-Freeman. Do not promise exact optimal codes.

source: Dowe, Gardner and Oppy (2007) Bayes not bust! Why simplicity is no problem for Bayesians, Brit J Phil Sci (draft)
finding: Worked example of Strict MML on a binomial: N=100 trials, uniform prior on p. The optimal code-book has just ten groups. Any result of 33 to 49 successes gives the same estimate, 0.41. The wide groups match the estimation error, so no precision is wasted.
numbers: Ten groups for N=100. Group estimate h5=0.41. Probability of exactly 41 successes at p=0.41 is 0.0809; of 33 successes 0.0218; of 49 successes 0.0216. The continuous prior becomes a discrete coding prior of ten values.
limits: Algorithm due to Farr and Wallace (2002); one parameter only.
agent_relevance: Shows the core MML idea: state a parameter only as precisely as the data can support. A simple rule for how much detail a claim deserves.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, equations (19) and (20): MMLD and Wallace-Freeman approximations
finding: Wallace-Freeman (1987) gives a practical formula for the message length: -log h(theta) + L + 0.5 log Fisher(theta) + (d/2)(1 + log kappa_d). If the Fisher term is crudely replaced by k log N, the formula reduces to something equivalent to BIC and to Rissanen's 1978 MDL.
numbers: d = number of parameters; L = negative log-likelihood; h = prior. MMLD instead minimises over a region R, using MCMC. Dowe argues the Fisher term should not be dropped.
limits: Needs a prior and the Fisher information; no closed form for complex models.
agent_relevance: The formula shows why 'more parameters' costs bits at a rate that depends on the data, not a flat penalty.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, section 6.4 Neyman-Scott problem and consistency
finding: Neyman-Scott: measure N people's heights J times each (say J=2) and infer all heights and the instrument noise. The ML estimate of sigma squared converges to (J-1)/J times the truth, so it is inconsistent. Bayesian MAP and the minimum expected KL estimator are also inconsistent (they over-estimate). Wallace-Freeman MML and the Ideal Group estimator are consistent.
numbers: JN data points for N+1 parameters; data per parameter bounded by J. For J=2, ML sigma squared tends to half the true value.
limits: Result proved by Dowe and Wallace (1996, 1997); cited via the chapter, not rechecked.
agent_relevance: Warning for any agent that adds one free detail per item: fit gets better but the estimate stays wrong.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, section 6.5 Lancaster panel-data problem
finding: In a panel-data regression, the Wallace-Freeman MML estimate gives what Lancaster calls the correct degrees of freedom N(T-1), apart from a negligible term. The ML estimate uses the wrong count.
numbers: y_it = f_i + x_it + u_it, i=1..N, t=1..T; message length reduces to a sum of squares with the N(T-1) correction.
limits: One worked example; no simulation table in the chapter.
agent_relevance: Independent route to the same lesson: counting the cost of each free parameter changes the answer.

source: Dowe, Gardner and Oppy (2007) Bayes not bust!, section 6.2.1 polynomial regression (results from Wallace 1997)
finding: Simulation of order selection for polynomial curve fitting: target sin squared, N=10 points, noise SD 0.61, signal/noise 10, 1000 cases. MML had an average squared prediction error (ESPE) of 0.1857; AIC had 15.8055. AIC never chose degree 0 or 1; MML did so 255 times. AIC chose the maximum degree 8 on 154 cases; MML on 10.
numbers: ESPE avg: MML 0.1857 (SD 0.2633); AIC 15.8055 (SD 63.8077). 95th percentile: MML 0.6075, AIC 306.5. AIC worst case more than 200 times MML's worst. Authors say 'orders of magnitude' on average over many other trials.
limits: Small N (10), chosen by an MML author; the draft says the gap shrinks with low noise and large samples. No independent lab repeated this table in the sources read.
agent_relevance: Strong small-data evidence that an MML-style penalty avoids overfit where a flat penalty fails. Relevant when the agent has few examples.

source: Dowe, Gardner and Oppy (2007) Bayes not bust!, section 6.2.2 autoregressive time series (Fitzgibbon et al 2004)
finding: Comparison of AIC, AICc and MML for choosing the order of econometric autoregressions. In all cases MML chose the order best; MML was the one most likely to under-estimate order; AIC was worst and most likely to over-estimate. MML had the smallest prediction error and AIC the largest.
numbers: Measure: mean squared prediction error on held-out period; no table reproduced in the draft.
limits: Reported second-hand in the draft; numbers not shown.
agent_relevance: Same direction as the polynomial result: MML is conservative and gives simpler models.

source: Dowe, Gardner and Oppy (2007) Bayes not bust!, section 6.2.3 cyclone prediction (Rumantir and Wallace 2003)
finding: Twelve model-selection methods compared for tropical cyclone intensity, choosing among 36 variables in a second-order polynomial. On simulated data MML reliably found the true model; AIC over-fitted. On real data MML found a parsimonious model and beat existing cyclone prediction techniques.
numbers: 12 methods; 36 candidate variables. AIC was not competitive enough to be tested on the real data.
limits: No numbers given in the draft.
agent_relevance: A real-data case where a compression criterion beat the field's practice; shows use outside toy problems.

source: Dowe, Gardner and Oppy (2007) Bayes not bust!, section 6.1.2 von Mises circular distribution (Wallace and Dowe 1993)
finding: For estimating the concentration of a circular (von Mises) distribution, Maximum Likelihood (and so AIC) was worst or equal-worst on every error measure, every true value and every sample size. MML was mostly best, otherwise nearly best. Gaps were largest for small samples. Same pattern for von Mises-Fisher on a sphere (Dowe et al 1996).
numbers: Error measures: bias, absolute error, squared error, Kullback-Leibler distance.
limits: Numbers not reproduced in the draft.
agent_relevance: Another small-sample case. Estimation, not only selection, is better under MML.

source: Dowe, Gardner and Oppy (2007) Bayes not bust!, section 6.2.4 gap or no gap
finding: Test case: data uniform on [0,1] versus uniform with a gap. The expected largest gap in N points is (log N)/N. If the gap is exactly that size, AIC wrongly prefers the gap model, and does so more and more surely. MML correctly prefers no gap and only accepts a gap near (2 log N)/N.
numbers: Expected average gap 1/N; largest gap about (log N)/N; MML threshold about (2 log N)/N. AIC overestimates the gap size, which gives infinite KL distance.
limits: Proof in the draft's appendix B; the problem was invented by the MML authors.
agent_relevance: A pattern test: ignore 'structure' that is the size random noise gives for free. Good rule against seeing patterns in noise.

source: Dowe, Gardner and Oppy (2007) Bayes not bust! (properties of SMML)
finding: Strict MML is invariant under one-to-one re-parametrisation (same answer in polar or Cartesian terms), is defined for any prior, and has not been shown to be inconsistent. The authors argue this answers a common objection to Bayes methods, and that Forster and Sober's attack on Bayesian simplicity fails.
numbers: Invariance: both estimator and message length are unchanged by one-to-one measure-preserving change of parameters.
limits: A philosophy-of-science argument; the debate with AIC supporters is not settled in this draft.
agent_relevance: Supports using a code-length score as a fixed yardstick that does not depend on how we name variables.

source: Wallace and Dowe (1994) Intrinsic classification by MML - the Snob program (AI94 proceedings, pp 37-44)
finding: Snob models each class with Normal (continuous) or multi-state (discrete) attributes. The hypothesis part of the message states: number of classes, relative abundance of each class, parameters of each class (to a precision about the size of their estimation error), and the class of each thing. Part 2 states every attribute value given its class. A new class is added only when its parameter cost is more than repaid by cheaper data coding.
numbers: Larger classes get more precisely stated parameters than smaller classes. Class label length = -log2 of relative abundance (Huffman). Programs only compute the length; no message is ever built.
limits: Description of the method; no accuracy table in this paper.
agent_relevance: A template for 'when to split a category': split only if the saving in coding items beats the cost of the new category.

source: Wallace and Dowe (1994) Snob (partial assignment and consistency)
finding: Total assignment of each item to one class makes the estimate inconsistent. Partial (probabilistic) assignment gives shorter messages: cost is -log P(x) with P(x) the sum over classes, rather than -log max_j p(j,x). With total assignment, two Normal classes whose means are less than 2.5 true SDs apart are fitted as one class however much data there is.
numbers: Threshold 2.5 SD (from earlier Wallace work). A coding trick uses the random-looking tail of an optimal message to assign items.
limits: Stated as a theory result; no simulation shown in this paper.
agent_relevance: Overlapping categories should be held as probabilities, not forced into hard boxes.

source: Wallace and Dowe (1994) Snob (significance in bits and applications)
finding: In Snob work, a difference of more than 5 to 6 bits (Wallace and Freeman 1987) or more than 10 bits (Wallace and Boulton 1968) in message length can be deemed statistically significant. Applications listed: depression classification, family clusters when a parent is terminally ill with cancer, word counts in 17th-century texts (Poisson module), protein dihedral angles (von Mises module).
numbers: Bits thresholds: 5-6 or 10. Several thousand protein angle sets under analysis in 1994.
limits: Thresholds depend on modelling conditions; no false-positive rate given.
agent_relevance: A usable stopping rule in bits: accept the more complex story only if it saves several bits.

source: Pilowsky, Levine and Boulton (1969) The classification of depression by numerical taxonomy, Brit J Psychiatry 115:937-945; Prior et al (1998) autism subgroups
finding: Early applications of MML-based classification to clinical data: depression subtypes (1969) and subgroups in the autistic spectrum (Prior et al 1998, with Dowe). Seen only as reference-list entries.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Papers not opened; only citations in the foreword and Snob paper.
agent_relevance: Shows the method was used on messy human data, but we have no replication data from these.

source: Dowe (2008) Foreword (footnote on Snob and protein structure)
finding: Applying Snob to protein structure data gave evidence that helices and extended strands form first and the 'other' turn classes form afterwards to fit them. Also: Wallace's unpublished 1982 outlier manuscript assumed two classes and partial assignment.
numbers: Cited work: refs 103 sec 6, 78 sec 5 p253, 283 sec 4.2 in the foreword's numbering.
limits: Reported from the author's memory; underlying papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Example of a discovery made by structure search with a compression score, not by a human hypothesis.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, section 6.7 MML versus MDL
finding: MML appeared 10 years and about 6 journal papers before Rissanen's MDL (1978). MML is Bayesian and states parameters to optimal precision; MDL (Normalised Maximum Likelihood) uses a Jeffreys 'prior' that can fail to normalise and depends on instrument scale. Grunwald and Langford (2004, 2007) showed some Bayes and MDL forms are inconsistent under misspecification; no inconsistency is known for MML. An attack on MML (Grunwald et al 1998) was later retracted.
numbers: Dowe: crude k log N reduces MML to BIC / early MDL. MDL 'completing the code' fails in simple cases (Wallace and Dowe 1999b).
limits: The chapter is written by an MML partisan; MDL authors do not agree on every point.
agent_relevance: Choose the MML-flavoured two-part code (with prior, with precision) rather than a bare parameter count.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Minimum description length
finding: Neutral summary of the differences. MML is fully Bayesian and encodes prior beliefs; MDL avoids assumptions about the data source. MML puts all parameters in part one and states each to optimal precision; MDL can move nuisance parameters into one-part codes. Statistical MDL is not computationally universal.
numbers: Coin example: 1000 fair flips cost exactly 1000 bits; 510 heads and 490 tails gives a biased-coin code that is still longer once the model is paid for, so no evidence of bias.
limits: Encyclopedia source; secondary.
agent_relevance: The coin example is a quick unit test for a 'bits to state a claim' check.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, section 6.6 Conjectures on consistency and invariance
finding: Conjecture 1: only MML and very closely related Bayesian methods are in general both statistically consistent and invariant. Conjecture 2: any non-Bayesian method that is both will be far less efficient. Extension to misspecified models: MML is expected to stay consistent. Dowe says he has seen no counter-example.
numbers: Conjectures from Dowe et al 1998, Wallace and Dowe 1999a, Dowe 2007, 2008.
limits: Unproven; Wallace himself doubted it, thinking a tuned method of moments might be consistent.
agent_relevance: Treat the claim that MML is uniquely sound as an open conjecture.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, section 4.1 inference versus prediction
finding: MML does inference: it picks the single best theory. Solomonoff does prediction: it combines many theories. Bayesian prediction often needs a mix, especially when two models of slightly different posterior give very different answers.
numbers: Not a numeric result; the chapter cites Wallace 1996b, 2005 sec 10.1; Tan and Dowe 2006.
limits: The split is a framing choice; MML's single theory can be worse for prediction.
agent_relevance: Our agent should keep one best explanation for reporting but may vote across several candidates for the final answer.

source: Dowe (2010) Handbook chapter, section 7.3 MML, inductive inference and intelligence
finding: Dowe argues that the inductive part of intelligence equals two-part compression (Dowe and Hajek 1997, 1998; Sanghi and Dowe 2003), and that plain one-part compression can lead to wrong models (as in the Neyman-Scott and gap cases). Intelligence also includes memory and deduction, which compression does not cover. Hutter's compression-equals-AI claim is later than Hernandez-Orallo's similar idea.
numbers: A chess player or proof checker uses mostly deduction and memory, little induction.
limits: Philosophical argument, no experiment.
agent_relevance: A counterpoint to 'compression equals intelligence' claims about LLMs: check both parts and what is left out.

source: Dowe (2008) Foreword (log-loss remark on boosting)
finding: Methods judged by right/wrong accuracy should also be judged by a probabilistic log-loss score. With a 50-50 target and many unrelated inputs, boosting can fit spuriously, leaving accuracy undamaged but giving an abysmal probabilistic score.
numbers: Argument by example, no figures.
limits: No experiment reported.
agent_relevance: Use log-loss or bits, not only pass/fail, when checking a confidence number.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Minimum message length
finding: MML is a Bayesian, information-theoretic method; first in Wallace and Boulton 1968; message = model plus data given model; parameter precision is part of the cost; Fisher information discretises continuous parameters; invariant and consistent on Neyman-Scott and factor analysis; does not need a Turing-complete language, unlike Kolmogorov complexity.
numbers: Applied since 1968 to decision trees, Bayesian networks, image compression and many learners.
limits: Short secondary page; no formulas.
agent_relevance: Quick reference only.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Inductive probability
finding: Evidence for a hypothesis H given facts F is the compression gained by assuming H: P(H|F) = 2^-(L(H) + L(F|H) - L(F)). A program of length L(K) bits has prior 2^-L(K). Kolmogorov complexity is not computable.
numbers: Each extra bit halves the probability.
limits: The page calls it a relative probability, not a true probability.
agent_relevance: A one-line formula: bits saved by the hypothesis equal log-odds in its favour.

source: Hlavackova-Schindler, Melnykova and Tubikanec (2023, v2 2024) Granger causal inference in multivariate Hawkes processes by minimum message length (arXiv 2309.02027)
finding: A recent MML application. In sparse cascade graphs with short time horizons, MML (MMLH) gets the highest F1 score for recovering causal links. Lasso-type and AIC penalties over-fit. MMLH is only slightly better than BIC.
numbers: Cascade setting, p=7, T=200: F1 MMLH 0.948 (SD 0.089), BIC 0.943, AIC 0.850, ADM4 0.773, MLE-ms 0.572, MDL-based MDLH 0.566, MLE threshold 0.410, random 0.130. p=20, T=200: MMLH 0.933, BIC 0.927, AIC 0.719, ADM4 0.694, MDLH 0.398, MLE-thr 0.099. T=700, p=7: MMLH 0.985, BIC 0.983.
limits: Gap to BIC is about 0.005 F1, within one SD. Priors were set very flat (b=10^5, c=10^-5), which makes MML act like BIC. Simulated data; one real set (G7 bond volatility).
agent_relevance: Shows modern MML can beat AIC and an MDL baseline, but plain BIC is nearly as good when the prior is flat.

source: Hlavackova-Schindler, Melnykova and Tubikanec (2024) arXiv 2309.02027, mid-dense setting and prior sensitivity
finding: Boundary condition: in the mid-dense setting (about 40% of edges for p=7), the MDL-based method MDLH has the best F1, and for short horizons MMLH is also beaten by ADM4 and thresholded ML. For T of 1000 or more MMLH approaches 0.9, MDLH about 0.95 and AIC about 0.92. MMLH still beats BIC at every tested prior setting. Lowering the prior constant b reduces F1 because false links appear, though true positives stay high.
numbers: Prior values b=4 and c=0.3. Figures from the paper's prose: MDLH near 0.95, AIC near 0.92, MMLH near 0.9 at T>=1000.
limits: Table columns were scrambled in text extraction, so only statements in the paper's prose are used.
agent_relevance: Failure case: when the true structure is dense, a code-length penalty that favours sparsity loses. Match the penalty to the expected density.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Chris Wallace (computer scientist); Dowe (2008) Foreword biography
finding: Christopher Stewart Wallace (1933-2004), Australian physicist and computer scientist. PhD Sydney 1959; the Wallace tree multiplier (1964); Foundation Professor of Computer Science (then Information Science) at Monash in 1968; ACM Fellow 1995. His book Statistical and Inductive Inference by Minimum Message Length (Springer, 2005, 432 pages) was published after his death.
numbers: In 1968 with David Boulton he built the SNOB program for unsupervised classification, the first use of MML.
limits: Biographical.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Monash Snob page (Dowe), Snob software history
finding: Snob (name joke: it makes 'arbitrary class distinctions') fits finite mixtures with Normal, multi-state, Poisson and von Mises attributes, handles missing data, and is Fortran. 1998: Wallace added spatial correlation (images). Later work added factor analysis (Edwards and Dowe 1998), t and Gamma distributions (Agusta and Dowe 2002, 2003), and a climate application (Visser and Dowe 2007, 2009).
limits: Software page; no benchmark numbers.
agent_relevance: Shows the line from 1968 clustering to modern mixture tools; the scoring rule never changed.

source: Wallace and Dowe (1999) Minimum message length and Kolmogorov complexity, Computer Journal 42(4):270-283
finding: Shows how MML relates to Kolmogorov complexity: the first part of the message makes a universal Turing machine act as if the data came from hypothesis H; the second part makes it write the data. The choice of machine is a Bayesian choice of prior.
numbers: No figures read; summary taken from the Dowe 2010 chapter.
limits: Paper not opened (publisher blocked).
agent_relevance: Link to the algorithmic subfield (C11 subfield 07).

source: Leads found but not opened: Learning logical rules using minimum message length (2025); Entropic strict MML and its connections to PAC-Bayes and NML (2026)
finding: A Semantic Scholar listing showed these titles. They suggest MML is used for rule learning and linked to PAC-Bayes. No abstract or result was read.
numbers: None.
limits: Could not open: rate limits.
agent_relevance: Follow up in a later pass; possibly relevant to program synthesis and generalisation bounds.
